title: AEPD (Spain) - PS-00426-2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A data subject complained to the DPA about the violation about the informational signage used and placed by Secritas (the controller) since 2011. The sign contains a logo, service descriptions, a caption referencing the recording of images and sounds, and a phone number to exercise the right of access and objection. The phone number included was a 902 premium-rate number which meant the individual calling would incur the costs.
In the course of the proceedings the controller acknowledged the use of the sign since 2011 and that the one presented during the investigation was not the only model of the signage being used. The controller further clarified that the new signs produced after the complaint, ceased to include the phone number and exercise of rights text, and any further production of the signs would also not contain this text.
The controller emphasised that due to logistical and financial constraints they were not able to remove or replace all the disputed signs. Furthermore, the controller’s website addressed two separate ways of exercising data protection rights, through an email address and a physical address.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA clarified that video surveillance for security purposes is subject not only to private security sector regulations but also the GDPR. In that regard, the DPA held that the controller as part of its business operations must prepare such signage in compliance with the GDPR. Considering that the controller has been installing this signage since 2011, the DPA held that since the GDPR’s entry into force the controller had been violating Article 12(2) GDPR. 
Furthermore, the DPA found that the controller advertises and encourages individuals to contact them for general inquiries through a 900 number which is free of charge to the caller. Nonetheless, the controller chose other means for contact when the matter dealt with data subjects exercising their rights. For that matter, the DPA held that the 902 number on the signage was deterring individuals from exercising their data subject rights, as the investigation demonstrated that most individuals seeking to exercise their rights opted for other contact methods.
Finally, the DPA rejected the controller’s argument that the processing fell within the scope of its usual business practices. Particularly because the DPA found that this did not excuse that aspects of the controllers processing activities were contrary to the GDPR.
The DPA held that the controller was liable for a violation of Article 12(2) GDPR which imposes the obligation on controllers to enable the exercise, by data subjects, of their rights. Therefore, the DPA imposed a €100,000 fine on the controller.

title: BGH - I ZR 227/25
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A credit information agency (the controller) provided the data subject access to information on their personal data stored by the controller by letter in October 2023. This letter stated that the data subject base score was 20.22 % of a possible 100 %. It also contained a table with the credit scores transmitted in response to credit inquiries over the past twelve months.
Following this, the data subject brought a lawsuit demanding access to information regarding the calculation of their credit scores. The regional court dismissed the lawsuit, and the data subject appealed this decision to the higher regional court. The higher regional court ordered the controller to provide access to the data subject’s base score, the weighting of criteria that most strongly influence the score, and information on which of the data subject’s personal data and other criteria were used to calculate the base score.
The controller appealed the decision of the higher regional court to the Federal Court of Justice and requested that the data subject’s lawsuit be dismissed.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The Federal Court of Justice overturned the decision of the appellate court and referred the case back to the higher regional court for a new hearing and decision.
First, the court held that the right of access under Article 15(1)(h) GDPR presupposes the existence of automatic decision-making pursuant to Article 22(1) GDPR. The court referred to the CJEU decision C-634/21 SCHUFA Holding (Scoring) and pointed out that Article 22(1) GDPR only applies if (i) a decision has been made, (ii) this decision is based solely on automated processing, including profiling and (iii) the decision produces legal effects concerning the data subject, or similarly significantly affects them.[1] 
The court followed the CJEU's reasoning in the aforementioned case and found that the controller automatically calculating a person’s ability to meet future payment obligations in the form of a probability value constitutes a decision based on profiling within the meaning of Articles 4(4) and 22(1) GDPR.[2] However, the higher regional court had not sufficiently assessed whether the decision significantly affected the data subject. According to the Federal Court of Justice, the third criterion is fulfilled if it depends to a significant extent on the credit scores calculated by the controller whether a third party to whom the respective score is disclosed establishes, carries out, or terminates a contractual relationship with the data subject.
Finally, the court held that the burden of proof regarding the cumulative requirements for the right of access under Articles 15(1)(h) and 22(1) GDPR rests with the data subject. In light of the principle of effectiveness under EU law, the court argued that the requirements for the burden of proof should not be set too high. It is sufficient that the data subject proves that the controller transmitted a credit score to a third party and that a decision detrimental to the data subject was made during the initiation or performance a contractual relationship with that third party in temporal connection with the transmission. If this is proven, there is a factual presumption that the third party’s decision was primarily attributable to the credit scores generated by the controller.


↑ CJEU - C‑634/21 - SCHUFA Holding (Scoring), margin number 43.

↑ CJEU - C‑634/21 - SCHUFA Holding (Scoring), margin numbers 44-46.

title: IP (Slovenia) - 0612-35/2026/4
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a notification of a data breach at a high school, after which it started an investigation. During a high school graduation celebration, where every student was informed beforehand one by one of their own results, a printed list of every students’ results was accidentally left on a table. Additionally, this list included personal data such as name, date and place of birth, personal identification number, etc.
The data was accessible to the students for a few minutes, after which a teacher intervened and put the list away. Some students photographed the documents, stating they only had photographed their own results. The teachers immediately demanded the deletion of these pictures, after which the students did so and declared they had not shared them with anyone else.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the school violated Article 5(1)(f) GDPR by exposing students’ personal data in a publicly accessible setting, and therefore breached the requirement to ensure appropriate security through technical and organizational measures.
However, the DPA also held that the school already implemented appropriate measures under Article 24 GDPR, and that the school acted promptly to mitigate the incident and fulfilled its breach-notification obligations. Additionally, the DPA stated that the breach was caused by a one-time employee mistake, and that the exposure was limited in duration and audience.
In conclusion, the DPA issued a warning under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR as the appropriate corrective measure.

title: CNIL (France) - SAN-2026-015
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
FNAC DARTY PARTICIPATIONS ET SERVICES (FDPS) and FNAC DIRECT (joint controllers) operated a mobile app that offered an online shop. Through trackers on the app, the controller tracked identifiers assigned by the controllers to the users, as well as information regarding users’ activity such as products viewed and purchased and the interest they have shown in certain products. This tracking took place even when the user selected “Continue without accepting” on the consent banner that was shown when accessing the app.  
The tracking served three purposes: firstly, the display of complementary products to the products viewed or purchased, to encourage users to buy additional products. Secondly, to display similar products to the products the user already searched for in order to improve the user’s search and help them identify the sought product more easily. Lastly, training the product recommendation algorithm to improve product recommendations. 
noyb filed a complaint with the DPA. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found a violation of Article 5(3) ePrivacy Directive that is transposed into national law by Article 82 of the Data Protection Act. These provisions hold that prior consent must be obtained before reading from or writing to the terminal equipment (computer, telephone, etc.) of the data subject. Therefore, prior consent should have been obtained in this case, which the controllers failed to do.
The exemptions to the obligation to obtain prior consent are not applicable. Article 5(3) ePrivacy Directive and Article 82 of the Data Protection Act provide for exemptions in case the operation has the sole purpose of enabling or facilitating electronic communication, or is strictly necessary for the provision of an online communication service at the user’s request. When a multi-purpose tracker is used, all purposes must fall within the scope of the exemption. The DPA held that this was not the case.
According to the DPA, commercial targeting cannot fall under these exemptions. However, the purpose of displaying complementary products is not strictly necessary for enabling or facilitating electronic communication or the operation of the service. Improving the product recommendation algorithm falls within the broader objective of commercial targeting that require the collection of consent.
The fact that the purpose of improving the search function could, depending on the implementation methods, be considered strictly necessary for the provision of the communication service requested by the user, and thus could fall within the scope of the exemption, is irrelevant. The tracking for this purpose cannot be separated from the purposes named above that do not fall within the scope of the exemption.
The DPA imposed an administrative fine of €6 m on FNAC DARTY PARTICIPATIONS ET SERVICES and €1 m on FNAC direct. It took into account the seriousness of the infringement because of the user’s express refusal to the tracking by clicking on the “Continue without accepting” button, and the substantial number of persons affected.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 745/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A data subject submitted a complaint to the DPA regarding the online dissemination of his personal data, collected as a result of his participation in a competitive selection process, on the Agency for Digital Italy’s (the controller) website. Particularly, the list of 15 candidates (including the data subject), which were eligible for and admitted to the oral exam, had been published. The data subject had contacted the controller requesting the removal of his personal data from the website.
The DPA initiated a preliminary investigation within which the controller removed the document from its institutional website within hours.
The DPA then initiated proceedings, and in the controller’s defence, they expressed that the published list only made reference to the candidates first name, last name and score. Furthermore, the controller’s representative stated that normally, the results of competitive selection procedures do not include candidate’s personal data but rather the unique identification codes assigned to the candidates. Therefore, controller claimed that the publication of the list was a result of operational oversight, that is, an accident. Ultimately, the controller had granted the data subject’s request and believed in good faith that they had dealt with the matter.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that although the controller was convinced that it had replaced the published document with the one which utilised the assigned unique identification codes of candidates, the information remained accessible online.
The DPA emphasised that national law only requires final rankings of competitive selection procedures to be published online, not provisional lists. Additionally, the DPA referenced the guidelines it had drawn up to ensure proper handling of personal data in such contexts, emphasising a balancing between transparency and the protection of privacy.
In light of the above findings, the DPA fined the controller €15,000 for the disclosure of the list of 15 data subjects who were admitted to the oral exam, in violation of the principles of lawfulness fairness and transparency, and data minimisations (Articles 5(1)(a) and (c) GDPR) and lacking an appropriate legal basis (Article 6(1)(c) and (e) GDPR).

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 746/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint by an employee of Poste Italiane S.p.A. (the data subject) after Deutsche Bank denied the data subjects loan application, and subsequently published on its platform that the data subject had outstanding payments, specified the amount and their net income. Importantly, this platform was accessible to all Poste Italiane S.p.A.’s staff which is responsible for loan application management, and the staff pf the Portacomaro Stazione Post Office of the Municipality of Asti.
The data subject expressed that submitting the form was necessary for a loan application, however did not include a field to enter their salary. This information was to be provided directly by Poste Italiane S.p.A., and that Deutsche Bank would only disclose the outcome of the verification to Poste Italiane S.p.A. which would then communicate it to the data subject. The data subject objected to the processing of their data and requested the erasure of such data from Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. granted the data subject their request, however the data subject deemed the responses unsatisfactory.
The DPA launched a preliminary investigation into the Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. (the data subject chose not to file a complaint against the latter) requesting clarification of the contractual relationship, respective roles in terms of data protection and privacy, and the data processing practices related to loan applications and the data exchanged between the two.
Deutsche Bank clarified that the relationship with Poste Italiane S.p.A. was governed by an agreement regarding a loan which could be extended to customers of Poste Italiane S.p.A. under certain conditions. Furthermore, for privacy purposes, in line with the aforementioned agreement the two of them act as independent controllers. Nonetheless, Deutsche Bank emphasised that it also acts as a processor for Poste Italiane S.p.A. concerning the data communicated to the latter regarding the evaluation criteria for a loan applicant. Conversely, Poste Italiane S.p.A. acts as a processor for Deutsche Bank as regards the data exchange concerning the outcome of the preliminary review of a loan application.
Moreover, Deutsche Bank explained that the process of applying for a loan occurs through separate systems and involves three phases. Deutsche Bank underlined that at the end of the decision-making process, the applicant receives the final outcome however no information about Deutsche Bank’s creditworthiness assessment is disclosed. This was to remain exchanged and processed solely between Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A.
Although initially having received a complaint by the data subject, the DPA made this an ex officio investigation. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that Deutsche Bank on the one hand independently determines the processing purposes and essential means related to the data subject’s creditworthiness analysis and has the sole authority to grant or deny the loan. Whereas on the other hand, Poste Italiane S.p.A. operates on a separate contractual relationship with the data subject and processes personal data for its own purposes. Ultimately, it was made evident to the DPA that the processing activities including the disclosure by Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A. fell within the scope of what is necessary for the performance of their respective contractual obligations or precontractual measures requested by the data subject (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR).
Therefore, the DPA held that the decision to designate each other (Deutsche Bank and Poste Italiane S.p.A.) as processors under Article 28 GDPR was contrary to the Article 4(8) GDPR, which defines a processor as the entity processing on behalf and under the instructions of a controller. Namely because the DPA held that the factual assessment of the relationship demonstrates that the disclosure of information between them is carried out by each of them for their own purposes. Ultimately, according to the DPA this makes them independent controllers.
Furthermore, the DPA found that Deutsche Bank’s privacy notice had not been properly worded. Specifically, it held that regarding the processing of data subject’s personal data for the promotion and placement of the loan, Deutsche Bank should have specified the recipients or categories of recipients of the personal data in accordance to Article 13(1)(a) GDPR. Moreover, the privacy notice lacked the additional information necessary to guarantee fair and transparent processing operations pursuant to Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. 
In light of the foregoing investigation, the DPA held that Deutsche Bank carried out processing operations in violation of Articles 5(1)(a), 13(1)(a) and 28 GDPR, and correspondingly imposed a fine of €33,000 on Deutsche Bank.

title: IP (Slovenia) - 06111-65/2023/12
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint by an employee against his former employer (data controller) regarding the handling of his work email during a period of prolonged absence. The data controller accessed the employee’s email traffic data and subsequently redirected all incoming emails to a shared mailbox accessible to a replacement employee. The data controller argued that the measure was necessary to ensure business continuity, since the employee held a key position in the company and his email address contained necessary information to provide their services. The data controller relied on Article 6(1)(c) and (f) GDPR for accessing the email address, and Article 6(1)(f) GDPR for redirecting. 
The employee argued that the measure was unlawful and disproportionate because an automatic out-of-office reply had already been configured directing senders to other employees, and less intrusive measures were available. Additionally, he argued that redirecting the emails amounted to continuous monitoring of his communications.
The DPA examined the one-time access as well as the ongoing redirection of the employee’s emails to another mailbox. The DPA dismissed the one-time access claim, since it had been completed before the complaint was filed. Regarding the email-forwarding, the data controller claimed it had conducted a legitimate interests assessment, however it did not provide evidence of this prior assessment.  

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the data controller violated Article 5(1)(a) and (c) GDPR, as well as Article 6(1) GDPR, by redirecting the employee’s email without a valid legal basis.
It clarified that the controller must be able to demonstrate that a legitimate interests balancing test was carried out before the processing occurred, and therefore accountability from the controller was not satisfied. Furthermore, the processing was not strictly necessary because less intrusive measures were available, such as relying on automatic replies and organisational measures. At last, the forwarding continued for the entire period until termination of employment, which exceeded what was strictly necessary to achieve the employer’s objectives.
Although the DPA found a violation, it did not order corrective measures because forwarding had already been ceased and the employee’s account had been already deactivated following the termination of his contract.

title: BVwG - W298 2298066-1
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
According to national law (§ 6(2) and (3) PartG 2012), donations to political parties are being published on a government website, including the name of individuals who donate more than €150 and, in addition to that, the postal code of individuals who donate more than €500.
A data subject donated €2,600 to a political party. Their name and postal code were published on the government website. 
The data subject filed a complaint with the DPA. The DPA held that the national law provided for a legal basis for the publishing of their name and postal code. The data subject appealed the decision to the Federal Administrative Court (Bundesverwaltungsgericht, the court).

Holding[edit | edit source]
The court had doubts as to the compatibility of the national provision with the GDPR and European and national constitutional law.
The court held that the processing of personal data in relation to a donation to a political party are special categories of personal data pursuant to Article 9(1) GDPR. While this information does not directly reveal the political opinion of an individual, the data allows the inference of a supposed political affiliation, depending on the amount of money donated. 
Article 6(3) GDPR provides that where the processing is based on national law, the national provision shall meet an objective of public interest and be proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued.
The court held that the aim of transparency and control by the public in the light of donations to political parties is a legitimate aim in that regard. 
However, the court had doubts whether the processing is necessary to pursue that aim. According to the court, the legal materials documenting the legislative process of the national provision do not indicate that the legislator adequately considered whether it is necessary to publish the name and postal code of donors to a wide public, or whether it is a less intrusive but equally suitable means to restrict access to the information to a limited number of persons, or to omit the postal code of the donor. The principle of data minimisation pursuant to Article 5(1)(c) GDPR requires the legislator to make such considerations during the legislative process. Furthermore, the legislator should have considered the specific nature of the personal data according to Article 9(1) GDPR.
For those reasons, the court has doubts as to the compatibility of the national provision with Article 8(1) CFR and Article 8 ECHR, and applied to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) to decide on the matter of compatibility.

title: IP (Slovenia) - SI – 0612-59/2024/8
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The Slovenian DPA (Informacijski pooblaščenec, “IP”) opened an ex officio inspection against a controller (name redacted) to check its use of cookies and similar technologies on its website under Article 225 of the Slovenian Electronic Communications Act (ZEKom-2). The inspection concerned whether users were clearly and comprehensively informed about the controller and the purposes of processing before data was stored on or accessed from their terminal equipment, and whether valid consent was obtained for non-essential cookies.
The DPA inspected the website twice using a browser and the EDPB website auditing tool. The first inspection found, among other things, that the cookie banner covered the content of the “Privacy and cookies” page and could not be closed without making a choice, so detailed information was not accessible before a decision. Also that the purpose of one cookie category (“Optional”) was not explained clearly and that the published cookie list did not match the cookies actually set (two session cookies were missing, and for necessary cookies only generic examples were given). Also the privacy and cookie policy stated that using the website already means agreeing to the policy, described analytics data as anonymous although it explained that a cookie identifier distinguishes unique users, stated categorically that no personal data is passed on to third parties or third countries although it mentioned the use of third-party services, and described the right to lodge a complaint with the DPA as an “objection”.
The DPA informed the controller of these findings and gave it 14 days to respond and remedy the deficiencies. The controller replied and made changes. A second inspection showed that the banner could now be closed without a choice, the “Optional” category had been removed, the purposes of the remaining categories were described more clearly, users were informed about how to change or withdraw consent later, and the two session cookies were no longer detected. The policy, however, still contained the statements on consent by use, anonymity, non-disclosure to third parties and the “objection” wording, and for two analytics cookies set after consent it did not state the provider or domain or whether third parties have access to the data.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that, despite the improvements made during the proceedings, the controller still did not provide users with fully clear, comprehensive and consistent information about its use of cookies and the purposes of processing, and therefore infringed Article 225(1) ZEKom-2. That provision requires users to be informed clearly and comprehensively about the controller and the purposes of processing, in accordance with data protection law, before they consent. The DPA assessed this information against the transparency requirements of Articles 12(1) and 13 GDPR and the definition of consent in Article 4(11) GDPR, to which Article 225(3) ZEKom-2 refers. It stressed that the remaining deficiencies concerned the content of the published information, not the technical functioning of the revised consent mechanism.
First, the policy did not state the provider or domain of the two analytics cookies or whether third parties have access to the data linked to them. Referring to the CJEU’s judgment in Planet49 (C-673/17), the DPA considered third-party access part of the information needed for clear and comprehensive notice. Second, the policy mentioned the use of a specific service while categorically stating that no personal data is passed on to third parties or third countries. The DPA expressly did not find that a transfer to a third country actually takes place, but held that this inconsistency prevented users from understanding the actual processing and that, where appropriate, the information required by Article 13(1)(f) GDPR must be provided and match the technical set-up. Third, the statement that mere use of the website means agreement to the privacy and cookie rules is incompatible with Article 4(11) GDPR, which requires a statement or a clear affirmative action. Even though the new banner allows an active choice, the wording creates a wrong impression of how consent is given. Fourth, the DPA held, with reference to Article 4(1) GDPR and Recitals 26 and 30, that analytics data cannot be presented as anonymous where cookie identifiers count as online identifiers, the policy itself explains that an identifier distinguishes unique users, and no anonymisation was demonstrated. Finally, the right to lodge a complaint with the DPA (Articles 13(2) and 77 GDPR) was wrongly described as an “objection”, although the right to object under Article 21 GDPR is a separate right.
The DPA ordered the controller to align the information on its website and its privacy and cookie page with the actual situation within 30 days of service, and to report to the DPA in writing, with evidence, immediately and at the latest within 5 days after implementation. It considered 30 days proportionate because the measures required verification and rewording rather than a technical redesign. No fine was imposed. The decision can only be challenged in an administrative dispute before the Administrative Court within 30 days, and a lawsuit does not suspend enforcement.
